subsubtopic: TIBET-ANNIVERSARY OF CHINESE OCCUPATION-DALAI LAMA'S PEACE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the thirty-seventh anniversary of the illegal and cruel Chinese occupation of Tibet. Yesterday 60 Tibetan monks were arrested in Lhasa by the Chinese army for simply shouting the name of the Dalai Lama. Last week at least 19 Tibetans were killed for pro-independence demonstrations.
This is the worst attack on Tibetan freedom since 1959 when 87,000 Tibetans were killed and the Dalai Lama fled to exile. High ranking Tibetans have appealed for world support. They ask the United Nations to support their cause, to know that they are suffering, and that their human rights have been trampled upon for 37 years. On September 21 in Washington the Dalai Lama proposed a five-point peace plan. I ask the Government and all Hon. Members to give serious consideration to this important cause.

subsubtopic: CLEAN WATER SUPPLY-AIM OF WATERCAN ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's uniqueness is expressed in many ways. One of these is that we are blessed with plentiful supplies of clean water. The same cannot be said of the world's poor countries. Two billion people face the daily challenge of finding clean, uncontaminated water, and 80 per cent of disease in the Third World is caused by dirty water.
Ready and easy access to abundant supplies of clean water is essential if the cycle of poverty is to be broken and economic prosperity is to emerge in these less fortunate countries.
Watercan is a Canadian non-profit voluntary agency, founded by Michael Lubbock, an 81-year old constituent of mine, whose aim is to increase the supply of clean water in the poorer regions of the Third World. Watercan's aims and strategies are simple and effective. It raises donations by including its pamphlets with municipal water bills. Our Government has offered $50,000 for Watercan's operating costs and will contribute $2 for every $1 raised by donations.
Watercan has not wasted any time in providing clean water for those in need. A donation has already been sent to Zambia to provide for a system of wells.
I would like to commend Michael Lubbock's efforts, along with those cities which have included Watercan's pamphlets with their water bills. I call on all Canadian municipalities to follow suit to help Watercan's worthy mission.

Mr. Speaker, since this is Family Week I would like the House to reflect for a moment on some of the special needs of Canada's farm families.
Low incomes, high stress, and lack of safe and affordable child care are all concerns according to the responses to a rural farm women's needs survey conducted in my constituency.
Their basic survival as farmers is a major concern. Low prices and high debt loads are contributing to family stress. With 40 per cent of the families reporting a straight loss or net incomes of less than $5,000, it is small wonder that few of their children are contemplating a career on the farm.
Some 50 per cent of the farm women responding were looking for an off-farm job, and most reported that they could not find one. These women are well educated and have training in a wide variety of fields. However, when the farm economy is badly hurting, jobs are disappearing in all the related fields in rural Canada.
If the Government really had a commitment to Canadian farm families, it would be clear on its farm family assistance

October 7, 1987
policy. It would announce the level of grains income assistance for the coming year and would provide a clearly understood rural day care policy.

subtopic: HIGH QUALITY OF CANADIAN GRAIN EXPORTS
HIGH QUALITY OF CANADIAN GRAIN EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tass News Agency reports that more than 40 per cent of the June to September grain shipments from the United States of America to the Soviet Union were infested with live pests and had to be fumigated on arrival.
In Canada, thanks to the excellent work of the Canadian Grain Commission, all our export sales are thoroughly inspected and certified to be of the highest possible quality.
The Entomology Section of the Commission routinely examines over 100,000 samples per year from farms, elevators, and ships and, if any cases of infestation are found, licences can be revoked.
If the Soviet Union or any other buyer wants assured high quality grain, Canada, with our thorough inspection and high standards, remains the logical source of supply.

subtopic: FREE TRADE-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ESTABLISH SPECIAL PROGRAMS FOR WOMEN BEFORE MID-APRIL
FREE TRADE-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ESTABLISH SPECIAL PROGRAMS FOR WOMEN BEFORE MID-APRIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I said that women heaved a sigh of relief when they heard that the free trade talks were stalled. This week, we have an agreement, and many women are once again feeling their initial concern.
When we realize that two-thirds of the workers in the industries affected by free trade are women, and 65 percent of the people working in the service industry are women, when we realize that women have a harder time getting access to training and retraining programs than men, and that in the United States, many states have abysmal labour laws and a ridiculously low minimum wage, and that poverty hits women hardest, what has our Government done for more than 52 percent of the population?
It is intolerable that a Government should negotiate an agreement and leave out women.
I am therefore asking the Conservative Government to introduce special programs for women between now and mid-April, so that women can adjust to this new situation and so
that half the population of Canada is not left behind when the train leaves the station.

Mr. Speaker, if any region in Quebec can meet the free trade challenge successfully, Abitibi-Temiscamingue can.
Local personalities, including Paul and Robert Arcand, Jean Perron and Guylaine Saucier, have many times expressed their faith in the benefits of free trade for our region. This very morning, Jacques Bibeau, Mayor of Rouyn-Noranda, Paul-Aurele St-Pierre, Mayor of La Sarre, and Jacques Leblanc, Mayor of Ville-Marie, told me personally that they supported the free trade treaty. In fact, Mr. Perron from La Sarre said recently in Rouyn-Noranda, and I quote: "This is a government initiative that deserves our attention. Free trade is something to look forward to." He went on to say: "As far as I can see, the protectionists, the people who are against free trade, are trying to hide their own inefficiency. It takes a lot of guts to say yes to free trade, and we do say yes to free trade!"
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that thanks to this new dynamism in our region, our farmers, forestry workers and miners will meet this great challenge with enthusiasm and leave future generations a legacy they can be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, as Canadians begin to examine the Conservative Government's misguided, hurried and patently unfair trade deal with the United States they are realizing that Canada has been put up for sale. Even formerly staunch supporters of the trade initiative are now telling this Government that the deal is a bad one for Canada and Canadians.
Roger Phillips, president of Ipsco, one of Canada's major steelmakers, told the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) yesterday that he could no longer support the trade pact because it does nothing to guarantee secure access to the U.S. market for Canadian steelmakers. Canadian steelmakers, he warned, will not be able to compete on an equal footing with their rivals across the border as a result of this flawed deal.
October 7, 1987

It is clear that Mr. Phillips cannot be duped by the Government's empty assurances that this deal is in Canada's interest. The Government should heed the judgment of Canadians like Roger Phillips, before it is too late.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the pathetic performance of the Liberals and the New Democrats during Canada's trade negotiations with the United States cannot pass without comment. First they told Canadians that our social programs would be up for grabs. Were they? Not a single one. Then they claimed that Canada's cultural industries would be sold out. Were they? Not one. Next they even suggested that our unemployment insurance program would be changed. Was it? Absolutely not. Finally they said that the Auto Pact would be dismantled. Was it? No. In fact it was strengthened.
So I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whose credibility is on the line? Certainly not this Government's whose initiative and courage have given us an historic trade deal that will ensure that Canada continues to prosper. Rather, I would suggest that Canadians think long and hard about the misleading and irresponsible disinformation circulated by Canada's not so Loyal Opposition and its socialist allies. Constructive actions speak much louder than deceptive words.
Our Government's record will bear the scrutiny of any honest Canadian. The same cannot be said of the Liberals and the New Democrats.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of the House what I believe to be a serious injustice in the way the Government is treating some of its civil servants. The injustice to which 1 am referring is the salary presently offered to registered nurses working for the federal Government.
At the present time a registered nurse makes three cents an hour more than a registered nurse assistant. I find this situation to be totally unacceptable. Representatives of nurses and the Professional Institute of the Public Service have met with the former Treasury Board President concerning this issue and were promised an answer by September 1. September 1 has long since come and gone and the registered nurses working for the federal Government are still being treated
unjustly and are still waiting. There are 900 hospital nurses in the service of the federal Government who need assistance.
I call upon the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) to act now. Any further delay and procrastination will only compound the present injustice.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF MANITOBA PREMIER
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF MANITOBA PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some things never change.
Was it any wonder last night we heard a voice crying alone in the socialist wilderness from Manitoba about free trade? We have come to expect Howard Pawley to take the reactionary socialist position of the rest of the New Democratic Party by protecting the status quo and resisting any positive change to our nation.
Howard Pawley and his group of NDP incompetents have made Manitoba an island of despair in Canada over the past three years. While Conservative policies have led the entire nation into new prosperity, the NDP in Manitoba have resisted at every step.
What is ironic and totally incomprehensible is that Mr. Pawley and his Government wish to seek and expand sales of Manitoba Hydro in the U.S.A., that Mr. Pawley and his Government wish to develop Manitoba potash and find a U.S.A. market, that Mr. Pawley and his Government in late 1984 tried to secure American investment to build a glass plant in his riding, that Mr. Pawley and his Government condemned the U.S.A. action of countervail duty on Canadian hogs, and yet do not favour a free trade pact which would secure these markets for Manitoba. He and his Government should resign.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Conservatives want Canadians to believe, falsely, I think, that the New Democrat opposition to free trade is based on a backward vision while they somehow are looking to the future. The contrary in fact is true. It is the Conservatives, with their backward look at the voodoo economics of the 18th and 19th century when free trade was a panacea.

October 7, 1987
Oral Questions
We are looking to the future. We believe in fairness for Canadians and for future generations. We have confidence in Canadians. We believe that Canadians can create jobs in Canada without becoming the 51st State of the United States.
Many Canadians want to see energy policies and conservation of non-renewable resources. This free trade deal would betray that trust. It means unfairness for Canadians in the future.
What about the Liberals? They have renounced the voodoo economics of the past but they have no alternative vision. We have and that is what we will be taking to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the socialist party has announced that he will send his jackals and hyenas throughout the country to fight against free trade. 1 would like all Canadians, each time they hear one of these doom and gloom prophets criticize free trade, to ask them these questions: Why is free trade good for the Oshawa constituency and has been applied there since 1965? Why are Oshawa workers much better paid than the national average? Why do retired automobile workers have an indexed pension plan?
The answer is that they have benefited from free trade since 1965. Ask any socialist Member why he does not want what has happened in Oshawa and what has been good for that region to apply to the rest of Canada.
We Canadians have to start asking questions to the socialists, to these frustrated members of our society. Let us ask them where they come from. They have always been parasites living off Governments, universities or the money of poor workers.

subtopic: FREE TRADE-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILLING TO HONOUR COMMITMENT MADE IN HALIFAX

speechtext:

In my opinion, it is obvious that I shall not be able to reach a free trade
agreement in a federal system such as we have in Canada without the support
and participation of the provinces affected.
We now know that several Premiers disagree with the agreement. We also know that several areas under provincial jurisdiction are affected by the free trade agreement. Is the Government willing to respect the commitment it made in November 1985 or will it forget that promise?

at all in the agreement itself because it met all their regional interests.

Who speaks for the Government? Is it the Prime Minister? The Minister of Finance? Or is the Government totally unprepared to come to grips with this vital issue and does not really know what it is doing?

readjustment program to compensate- for free trade. On Tuesday the Premiers said they had never heard of such a program and the Minister of Finance did contradict the Prime Minister.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am now in a position to advise the House that there are programs already in place to trigger the employment adjustment mechanism. Some 5 million Canadians per year have changed jobs, one way or another, and we have the necessary mechanism to relocate and properly help these people. Now, as far as the Canada-United States deal is concerned, both the assessment and review of the mechanism provided for under this deal will take place. No job will be lost before January 1, 1989. Nothing will be done until then. My Department, together with all the others, will carry out a series of analyses and, on the basis of our findings, the necessary measures will be implemented. But what differentiates us from the Liberals is the fact that we study a situation before acting upon it whereas they used to act first, and we have had to face the consequences.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked questions about why the Government gave up our sovereign control over pricing and security of supply in energy. Today I have a question about the loss of sovereignty in the investment field.

October 7, 1987
Oral Questions
I will direct my question to the Minister for International Trade. According to a study produced by Statistics Canada and released just over an hour ago in Edmonton, for every $1 billion in profits between 1978 and 1985 Canadian companies created 5,700 new jobs. For the same $1 billion of profits during the same period of time U.S. firms created the grand total of 17 jobs.
Given the alarming significance of this data, is this not a time when we should be, if anything, increasing our monitoring of the performance of foreign firms in Canada instead of giving up our sovereignty in this field?

You will recall that when the Government took office we changed FIRA to Investment Canada and changed the thresholds. There was record investment after that. We are changing the thresholds again.
While I am not aware of the particular study to which the Hon. Member has referred, I can give him a different set of statistics. We have created one million new jobs since we took office and last year we had a record $6 billion worth of investment. Surely the two are connected.

The Canadian firms that are making the profits are indeed reinvesting, but the foreign firms that are making the profits overwhelmingly are taking the profits out of Canada. That is the point.

firms are investing in America, in percentage terms, than are investing here. We think this is a good agreement, and that it will create new investment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the week of October 4 to October 10 has been declared by the International Social Security Association to be the week of international co-operation in social security. During this week, which is also the sixtieth anniversary of the association, countries around the world have been asked to reflect on the benefits which each has gained by working with others toward the development of social security systems that more fully meet the needs and hopes of our citizens.
The Canadian member institutions of the International Social Security Association, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Regie des rentes du Quebec, have played a very active role in the work of this vital association, and we will continue to do so.
Canada, as a nation made up of people whose origins can be traced to virtually every country in the world, recognizes the importance of international co-operation in social security. The most concrete and best known form of co-operation is, undoubtedly, the social securities agreements which Canada has concluded in recent years and which bring benefits to thousands of our fellow citizens.
It has been my honour to sign 11 agreements in my term as Minister of National Health and Welfare. These agreements were concluded with Austria, Barbados, Denmark, Finland, the Federal Republic of Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Saint Lucia, Spain and Sweden. I look forward in the ensuing months to signing more.

October 7, 1987

I know that all Members of this House join me in congratulating the International Social Security Association for its accomplishments in its first 60 years and in wishing it well in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, during this week of international social security, I applaud the Minister for his achievement of 11 social security agreements with various governments. I know they will be of particular benefit to Canadians who have come from other countries.
I want to raise a related matter of great importance to the future social security of Canadian citizens. Since this week also is National Family Week, I remind the Minister that Canada is a signatory to the International Covenant for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Article II of this covenant states that governments are required to provide for the basic needs of their citizens and to strive for continuous improvement of living conditions.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan, provinces are required to provide financial aid or assistance to any person in need in an amount that takes into account his basic requirements. How then does this Government explain the continuing increase of poverty among Canadian families with young children? How can we tolerate the fact that one out of every five of our children is being raised in poverty?
Consider what it means to be born into poverty, to be raised poor, to bear your children in poverty and to die poor. It means being shortchanged at birth by inadequate pre-natal care, not getting enough to eat, and being sick more often than other kids. It means entering the school system already seriously disadvantaged, being labelled "slow" because your hair does not shine, your eyes do not sparkle and you cannot sit still because you have had no breakfast. For girls it usually means having babies and repeating the cycle. For boys it usually means dropping out of school, heavy drinking, drug abuse and getting into trouble with the law.
In Canada we have condoned a situation of national child neglect. The decreasing incidence of poverty among the elderly proves beyond doubt that Government policy and programs can make the difference. I call upon the Government to turn its attention immediately to developing a comprehensive family policy that will provide some fairness and honesty for Canadian families and particularly for Canadian children who are poor.

In fact, I believe that that Party made the commitment on many occasions to end the kind of discrimination that currently exists with respect to the federal Government in our own social security system
dealing with single seniors, and with people who are separated and divorced who are not eligible for a spouse's allowance as a result.
I think for the Minister to make a great week, along with the commitment that he is making to social security internationally it would behoove him to stand up in the House and, rather than make an announcement in very glowing terms about what is happening across the world, say that he is prepared to end the discriminatory practices of the Government toward senior citizens. I do not think the battle against poverty among senior citizens has been won. I do believe that we are also launching a battle to fight the kind of poverty that is facing one child in five in Canada.
This evening I will be presenting a motion in the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare that we have an in depth study of poverty among children across the country. I do not think we can trade them off one against the other. We have to recognize that as a society we should be protecting our helpless and our defenceless. That includes our elderly and our children. I think the Minister would be far better in this House today were he to make an announcement regarding an end to his discriminatory policy with respect to senior's pensions.

Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte Marie (Mr. Malepart), has said many times that as far as allowances and old age security are concerned, the policy is discriminatory, and if the Minister really wants to make this a week when Canadians could rejoice in our social security policy, he should announce in the House today that he will drop a policy that discriminates against the elderly and against persons who are single, divorced or separated, since it does not give them the same benefits as persons who are married or widowed. Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure and the obligation under Standing Order 106 to present to the House some petitions. REFERENCE TO FORMER PREMIER OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I will simply to refer the House to page 9724 of Hansard where, in an exchange with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), I was referring to the past Premier of Alberta, a man with whom philosophically I disagree, but on a personal basis, a man with whom I have been friends for many years. I referred to him as Peter Lougheed and that is how I have always referred to Peter Lougheed. When I talk to him personally, I call him that, and they have written here "Low-heed".
I just do not want Hansard to reflect in any way negatively against the past Premier of Alberta. As a fellow Albertan, 1 particularly feel slighted that Hansard would have done this. However it is partly my fault because I did not read the "blues". If I had looked at them, I would have picked that up. In British Columbia, when we refer to Lougheed Place or Lougheed Mall or Lougheed Highway, that is the way we pronounce it, and if they spell it "Low-heed", it is intended as no slight against the past Premier of Alberta.

subsubtopic: CRTC-ALLEGED ERRONEOUS INFORMATION-CLOSING DATE- MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I now have a ruling to bring to the Chamber. On September 23, the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) raised a complaint with the chair alleging that certain actions and/or lack of action by the Canadian Radio Television Commission amounted to a breach of the privileges of the Hon. Member.
After hearing the case put forward, I said in part that the Hon. Member may not have a question of privilege, but I added, and I quote what I said on that day: "It most certainly is a complaint." Regretfully, I have to repeat that I am still of that mind. I think there is a complaint and a very real one.
While I will not comment on the Hon. Member's words when he talked about the "cavalier and inneficient manner of the operations of CRTC", on the facts presented, the Hon. Member for Kootenay West has a valid complaint and reason to be upset and angry.

As was said when the subject was raised, some simple changes in the regulations governing applications for rate changes would be sufficient to prevent this kind of frustration.
I do not think I need go into the various definitions of privilege found in the authorities May, Bourinot and Beau-chesne, but this type of problem is not covered by them. I will, however, refer Hon. Members to Citation 16 and Citation 17 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition.

I must therefore conclude, with all due respect, that the Hon. Member does not have a question of privilege.
October 7, 1987



I would add that this does not leave the Hon. Member without recourse. This fact needs to be emphasized. The recent reforms adopted by the House allow Members to pursue such matters vigorously, not only in one of the several standing committees but also under Private Members' Business. The Hon. Member for Kootenay West has made his point forcefully but, I repeat, it is with regret that the Chair cannot take any further action and the matter raised cannot go forward under a finding of prima facie privilege.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for his co-operation and patience in waiting for this ruling. I would like to be able to help him with his particular problem but, regretfully, I cannot under the concept of privilege. However, I hope the frank comments of the Chair might be helpful to the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, I begin my remarks on the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord by recalling that the last two times I had an opportunity to speak on the Constitution was, first, in the fall of 1980, and
again in 1981 at the time of the last constitutional upheaval, you might say.
I recall, and I say this not by way of excuse but by way of illustrating something, I hope, profound, that I was much more concerned to have a prepared text at that time than I am now. What I mean to illustrate by that is that over the years since 1980-81 I feel that what Members of Parliament have to say about constitutional matters has become less and less important. I want to illustrate that, if I might, by talking about some of the developments since then.
First, some would argue that the effect of the Charter of Rights we passed at that time has been to take decisions away from Parliament, which might otherwise have been made there, and placed them in the courts. Of course many people feel that is a good thing rather than a bad thing. However, the fact of the matter is, no matter how you feel about it, there are things being decided elsewhere which at one time would have been decided here in Parliament.
Second, if the free trade agreement comes to be a fact of Canadian life, many things that would have been open to Parliament to decide will, of necessity, be decided in the continental market-place and no longer by Parliament.
That is wrong.

So I feel as a Member of Parliament that my role, and that of Parliament itself, and the Canadian Government for that matter, will have been diminished.
Third, I also feel that the process surrounding the Meech Lake Accord has diminished the role of Members of Parliament. I want to preface my remarks by saying it is my intention to vote for the Meech Lake Accord. Let there be no confusion on that account. However, I feel that the process which has attended the Accord has set some very dangerous precedents with respect to the role of Members of Parliament in constitutional change.
It has been called executive federalism. Whatever you want to call it, the fact is that 11 people, the provincial Premiers and the Prime Minister, can arrive at agreements which profoundly affect the future of the country and then have Parliament put in the position, as we have been put, of not being able to amend what was decided by those 11 persons.
My support for the Accord was much more comfortable support in the early days when I thought Parliament might have an opportunity to amend the Accord. I thought the committee process might be a place where some of the obvious flaws in the Accord might be remedied.
The first flaw, of course, that comes to mind is the obvious injustice done to northern Canada by virtue of the requirement that there be unanimity with respect to the admission of new provinces. For the life of me I cannot understand why that was incorporated in the agreement and why, when there is almost universal agreement on the injustice of that provision, the agreement could not have been opened up to provide for that
October 7, 1987

particular amendment. I suppose it has something to do with the politics of it, I do not know. I suppose there are perhaps some Premiers who feel they did not get all they wanted and that if somehow the agreement were to be opened up, then new political pressures would be put on them to open up the agreement to get what they are being criticized for not getting. I understand that, but surely to God, when it comes to so obvious an injustice as that done to northern Canada, we should have been able to do it.
With respect to my support for the Accord, I want to say that I am going to be voting for it because at the end of the day, having heard all the arguments, certainly having been convinced of the imperfection of what is before us, I still think a Canada which accepts this Accord and goes beyond it to new constitutional evolution will be better than the Canada which would exist if this agreement were to fall apart.
That is an over-all judgment which every Member of this place has to make for himself or herself, and which political Parties also have to make. I emphasize that it is an over-all judgment. It is not a question of how and to what degree various Members are committed to the rights of aboriginal peoples or the multicultural nature of Canada or the equality rights in the Constitution or the importance of federal leadership in social policy, or whatever is on the great long list of concerns people have about this Accord. It is a question of people having to make an over-all judgment about what would be best. It would be easy for Members of Parliament, except perhaps those in Government, to say that we can vote against it on these grounds and therefore be absolved of any responsibility for the consequences of the imperfections of the agreement which become known in the future.
However, I think we have the responsibility to ask ourselves what we would do if our vote made the difference. Would we prefer the Canada which would result from the breakdown of this agreement or the Canada which would result from this agreement? My judgment at this time is that 1 would prefer the Canada which would result from the agreement. I hope that history proves me right. It is in the nature of constitutional debate that everyone has the responsibility to make his or her own decision.
I spoke earlier of my fears as a Member of Parliament about the growth of executive federalism. The current Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) organizes First Ministers' conferences by putting the Premiers into a room without their advisers or any backup, and there is no record kept. The Prime Minister is the only one who has any say about what the draft statement will look like. The Prime Minister goes out before the Premiers and has his little show with the media. The Premiers are not allowed to comment until some time after. From what I have heard from some who have participated, the whole process is quite orchestrated. This is no way to run a country. I hope this is peculiar to the style of the current Prime
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Minister and will not be endemic to First Ministers' conferences which will be institutionalized.
I would like more parliamentary participation to be institutionalized in constitutional negotiation and debate. I know the committee made some recommendations in that regard. I would like to call attention, as I know others have, to the proposal made by John Holtby for a more comprehensive parliamentary and legislative exercise which would include members of the legislatures of Canada on a umbrella-like committee. I recommend that proposal to Members who are interested in thinking about how parliamentarians and legislators can be more involved.
I want to speak a bit about the business of unanimity, and point out some of the ironies which attend constitutional policies and debates. I recall the debate in 1980-81 about the amending formula. It sometimes happens that people, by virtue of their vehemence against something, end up with a situation which is actually worse than that which they were attacking and which actually conforms more to what they were attacking than to that with which they started out.
For instance, I recall that people in the Prairie provinces in 1980-81 were very concerned about the amending formula proposed by the then Liberal Government which would have given Quebec a veto. By the way, the veto power which Quebec has under the Meech Lake Accord is much less than that previously proposed veto power. It has a veto only with regard to federal institutions rather than with regard to everything. That should be kept in mind by people who may be concerned about the veto of Quebec, as well as the veto of other provinces on federal institutions.
The people of the Prairie provinces were very concerned about Quebec having a veto. That same amending formula provided that any two western provinces could prevent something by not agreeing to the original veto which was provided for in that amending formula., As a result of objections to that particular formula we ended up with another formula which provided that two-thirds of the provinces comprising 50 per cent of the population could veto something. Under that formula something could be done in Canada without the consent of any of the Prairie provinces. That has always struck me as ironic.
It is also ironic that, thanks to two very significant political figures in our history, Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Diefenbaker, the "one Canada" heroes, the notion of any special veto for Quebec was made so anathema that when the Premiers went to Meech Lake many of them knew that for domestic political reasons if Quebec was to get any kind of veto over anything they had to have it too.
The tremendous political irony is that by creating the political context which they did, one could argue that Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Diefenbaker set the stage for the very kind of Canada which they claimed to be so much against. In fact, that is not the kind of Canada which they were either for or against because somewhere along the line the proposition got

October 7, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
sort of transmogrified into a situation in which all the provinces now have a veto with regard to certain matters. That is an incredible irony which should not go unremarked upon.
There is another thing which amazes me with regard to the principle of unanimity. We are about to enter into a constitutional situation in which unanimity will be required with regard to federal institutions. Yet, through the free trade agreement, the Government proposes to change the very economic constitution of this country without unanimity, without the approval of at least five of the ten provinces, and without even the requirement of a vote in Parliament. There may be a vote, but there is no requirement for one. It is a shortcoming of our system that something as important as the economic constitution of the country can be changed in the way in which the Government proposes to change it without a shred of unanimity, without even a consensus.
I know that other Members of Parliament, particularly some of the Conservative persuasion, will disagree with me, but I hope they will hear me out. I feel as though my country was sentenced to a slow death on Sunday morning. I believe that in time we will see the erosion of everything that I value about Canada as it is and as I thought it could become through the political process and the building up of an independent Canada on the northern half of North America.
I feel as though Meech Lake has all of a sudden become irrelevant. I have the sickening feeling in the pit of my stomach that it will not really matter any more, if the Government gets away with what it has in mind. In the offing is a process whereby Canada as we know it will come not to exist in any event, and, for example, whether the provinces or the federal Government appoints Senators is trivial in the long run. That about which I speak will not, of course, happen over night and that is what makes this debate on free trade so difficult. Again, it is a question of judgment as to what will arise out of any particular decision.
When I spoke on the Constitution in 1980 and 1981, I did not talk only about the need to patriate the Constitution but the need to patriate our economy. While the Liberals made some effort to patriate our economy through the National Energy Program in the following years, we are seeing the complete opposite now, where our economy is being exported by integrating it so profoundly into the American economy and North American market.
I want to deal with aboriginal rights. I was one of those in 1980 who was warning my Leader and others that I would not vote for the package as it was until it included aboriginal rights. I feel very good about that aspect of my political life, that we were able to achieve that recognition. While it was not as full and complete as we wanted, nevertheless I recall being part of the process whereby the Government of the day had to bend in order to get the kind of approval it wanted for that patriation package.
In my opinion, aboriginal rights are not endangered in any way by this particular Accord. I believe that we will only achieve a truly just relationship with native people when we, as a society, truly repent for the way we have treated native people. Constitutions will not achieve that, nor will the courts or many other mechanisms that are used. It will be a matter of political will, public opinion, and a change in the consciousness of Canadians. Quite frankly, I despair whether that change will ever happen, but that change in consciousness and political will is necessary in order to meet the wishes of the native leadership in this country.
I want to deal with one other issue in the minute I have remaining, and would hope that Hon. Members would indulge me for a few more minutes. It concerns the cynicism of the observations made about the various political parties with respect to Meech Lake. I speak particularly of the cynicism which has attended the NDP position on this matter.
Those who are seriously concerned about our position should review the history of NDP policy with respect to Quebec. They will see, as pointed out by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) yesterday, that the New Democratic Party's position now with respect to Quebec and the constitutional discussions has its roots in the very formation of the Party back in 1961. It is very cynical and wrong for journalists or others, including the general public, to say that the NDP is agreeing to the Meech Lake Accord because we are high in the polls or want support in Quebec.
This reflects a certain psychology that takes over political commentary. I have seen it happen with respect to other things since we began to do very well in the polls. For instance, some journalists have commented about the new suits I am wearing, when they are exactly the same suits I have been wearing for the last two years. Another example was when people thought that the reason my Leader was angry about the behaviour of one of my colleagues when President Reagan was here was that we were high in the polls. I can tell you that when I wore a black arm band when President Reagan was here in 1981 I was chewed out by the Leader, and we were low in the polls at that time.
There are principles which we hold whether or not we are high in the polls. Our high standing in the polls did not stop the New Democratic Party from taking what was perceived as an unpopular position with respect to refugee legislation. Our standing in the polls did not affect our position with respect to amendments to the drug patent laws even though they were popular in Quebec. That did not change our position, because we have principles.
One of our principles has been to recognize Quebec as a distinct society. It is a principle that goes back far into the history of the Party. Anyone who believes that what we are doing is a reflection of political opportunism is dead wrong.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member found it necessary to conclude his remarks by trying to explain away

1 suggest to the Hon. Member that it is because of statements like that that Canadians really wonder about the NDP position and perhaps about the Hon. Member's position. Mr. Speaker, 1 do not think it is either obvious or inconsistent. At the time of patriation, if certain language was not built into the Constitution, it would be of grave danger, indeed, to their rights.
I believe that this particular constitutional change neither advances nor retards the possibility that aboriginal peoples will get the justice which they seek within Canadian society. It is my understanding of the position they put before the committee that they were legitimately concerned that they would somehow be taken off the constitutional agenda by not having built into this Accord the provision for more constitutional conferences.
I certainly do not think that we have seen the last of constitutional conferences on aboriginal rights, even if there is no such provision in the Accord. That is not something which

is prohibited by the Accord. That is, pursuant to what I said earlier, something that will be created by the political process and by the political will to deal with those problems, whether it be through conferences or whatever the process may be.
I do not feel badly about the position that I have taken in this respect. Member who is a member of the reform committee of the House of Commons is whether in his judgment that kind of accepted recommendation, that is, accepted by all Parties, will have an impact on the Government, particularly in view of the fact that they have recommended what George Erasmus asked for, namely, a constitutional conference beginning in 1990.

Mr. Speaker, just on that point, I think that there are two questions to deal with, of course. The recommendations of the committee with respect to aboriginal claims, and also with respect to funding, ought to be followed by the Government. But I am beginning to be concerned that a Government which has made so much of parliamentary reform since its coming into office in 1984, and for that matter a Prime Minister who has made so much of parliamentary reform, is starting to develop a very bad record with respect to paying attention to the unanimous recommendations of committees. I would think that in their heart of hearts this should concern some of the Tory back-benchers, even though they might not want to admit it. There were the unanimous recommendations of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs with respect to food irradiation which have been completely ignored by the Government. There are the recommendations of the committee with respect to the matter under discussion, but also with respect to other amendments. There are other examples as well which dim the hope of those who were involved in parliamentary reform, that

a renewed committee system, and renewed political life in the committee system of this House, that this would happen through the Government actually paying heed to the recommendations of committees. Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands

Canso): Mr. Speaker, I want to say, first, that it is with a great deal of honour that I participate in this debate on what is an historic constitutional Accord, perhaps a milestone of governments in the last number of decades. It is an important debate because it focuses on the unity of our country. It focuses on the vision that we have as Canadians of our country and where we would like it to go.
We have heard a great deal in the course of this debate about the Accord, what it should say, what it does not say, and what are its strengths. Before we But to make look at the terms of the Accord we must understand what is the issue. We must understand the political, legal and constitutional context in which we as a country find ourselves in 1987.
What is the issue? Surely, the issue that faces all Members of this House and all Canadians is whether or not we as a country can accommodate Quebec within our constitutional family. We must ask ourselves whether we have the flexibility, the understanding, the commitment and the political will to reach out to the people of Quebec as we promised to do. In the 1980 referendum, Quebecers voted to stay within this country. They voted by a narrow margin to stay within this country. Fully 40 per cent of the people of Quebec voted to leave Canada as we know it today. Approximately 50 per cent of the French-speaking Members from Quebec voted to leave.
That is hardly a recommendation for the manner in which this country has been governed. It is hardly a recommendation for previous governments that have attempted to reconcile the national interests with the legitimate aspirations of the people of the Province of Quebec.
There are those who have said and will say that the question of 1980 was somehow not truly known to the people of Quebec when they voted, that it was a slanted question. But those who make that argument considerably underestimate the intelligence and awareness of the people of Quebec.
How could the people of Quebec participate in debate for months and years about the future of their province and not know what the question was when they went into the voting booths to vote yes or no? That is an argument which I cannot accept, and which somehow implies a certain degree of inferiority on the part of the people of Quebec. In fact, if anything, the people of Quebec have superior instincts in the political field.
The 1980 referendum was a request from the people of Quebec for Canada to adapt the Constitution, to allow the province to evolve within the Canadian family. But what happened? What followed was a series of actions by the national Government, and finally in concert with the provinces, which excluded Quebec, decisions were made about the fundamental nature of this country, about the future of the country, without the consent of the Province of Quebec.
There are those who will say, We would never have gotten the consent of Premier Rene Levesque and his separatist government that ruled the Quebec of the day. What they seem to ignore is that the National Assembly of Quebec voted unanimously to reject the terms of that Accord. The terms of 1981 and 1982 were not acceptable to any member of the National Assembly of Quebec, not just to the separatists that sat in the National Assembly. That is the situation that faced this country, that was part of this country until 1984.
In 1984, our present Prime Minister outlined to the people of Canada that he was committed to reconciling Quebec but reconciling Canada to Quebec as well. He said he was interested in national reconciliation, constitutional reform, and making the evolution of this country a top priority of the Government. What followed then were discussions, after his election as Prime Minister, with the Premiers.
Finally, in August of 1986, the 10 provincial Premiers and the Government of Canada decided that the Quebec issue was the primary issue that had to be addressed at First Ministers' constitutional meetings. That is why earlier this year the Premiers came together and were able to reach an accord. What followed August of 1986 were months of preparation by the Ministers in the respective provinces. This deal was not a rush deal. There are those who say that it was reached in two days. Those people who make that criticism are acknowledging only their ignorance of political and constitutional affairs. If they knew nothing about the negotiations that preceded the meetings of the spring that resulted in this Accord, they are simply admitting that they did not take the trouble to be informed.
The Accord of 1982 was imperfect in that it left Quebec out. The Accord of 1987 brings Quebec in. In my opinion, criticism of the process is unfounded. What about the deal? That is what truly interests Canadians. They are pleased to have Quebec within the constitutional family, but they will also ask, "Just what did it cost us?" In my view, it did not cost Canadians. Canadians only win as a result of the Meech Lake Accord. They win a united country.
Let us look at some of the terms of the Accord itself. In the Accord there are two new rules of interpretation. One is the recognition of Quebec within Canada as a distinct society. Some will say that that confers upon Quebec the right to pass laws, and say that it is a distinct society, therefore, it can do a,
October 7, 1987

b, or c. But the legal opinions are quite to the contrary. This is merely a rule of interpretation.
It states in the agreement that "the Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with . .. in other words, these are rules of interpretation. These are not grants of legislative powers. The Charter of Rights today provides that the Charter of Rights shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the reality of this country; that certain things can be done consistent with the rules of a democratic system. The reference to a distinct society is merely read in collateral and in conjunction with that reference.
What about the English minority in Quebec? The Accord also provides that Canada has dualism. In Canada there are English-speaking Canadians in a minority in Quebec, and French-speaking Canadians in a minority in many other provinces. To this point in time provinces that had rejected the concept of official bilingualism and a commitment to accepting and preserving the bilingual nature of the provinces have accepted in this Accord that as a fundamental characteristic of this country they will preserve its dualistic nature.
What about the powers of the legislatures and the Government of Canada? Again, the Accord states that nothing shall derogate from the powers, rights, or privileges of Parliament, the Government of Canada, or the legislatures or Governments of the provinces, including any powers, rights, or privileges relating to language. That is a very clear indication of the agreement that was reached by the Premiers.
What are some of the other terms? There is a reference and a decision made that the provinces may nominate persons to the Senate, and that the Government of Canada then will make a selection based on those nominations. There are those who say that we are giving away the shop; we are giving to the provinces control of the Senate. The appointment rests with the Government of Canada, but more basic than that is the reality that the Senate belongs to no government. It does not and should not belong to the Government of Canada. It is a national institution that belongs to all Canadians and is designed to reflect the co-operative and federal nature of this country. What a better way than to have joint appointments to the Senate to reflect this reality. Why should the Government of Canada be the sole appointing body to the Senate? In addition, there is a commitment to effect reform of the Senate.
In my view those who argue that somehow the Government of Canada is weakened, do not understand the federal nature of this country. They do not understand the agreement that was reached in 1867, or the agreements that followed that brought in other provinces. Those provinces agreed that this was a federal system of government; that the provinces had roles to play, but that these roles were protected by the Constitution and that no attempt would be made by the national Government to undermine that commitment in our constitutional documents.
A lot is also heard about the immigration agreement, that Quebec can somehow have a say in the nature of immigration
Constitution Amendment, 1987
into that province. This is not new ground. For a number of years the Province of Quebec has been a party to an agreement with the Government of Canada under which both Governments agree that the Province of Quebec has a role to play and a say in the nature of the immigration as it affects that province. That is not new.
It is also not new that there are amendments to the Supreme Court of Canada. In this regard, I hear and read some amazing comments. Because the provinces have a right to make nominations to the Supreme Court of Canada, we hear some people state that the Supreme Court of Canada will be an instrument of the provincial Governments, and that we will have pro-provincial decisions from the Supreme Court of Canada. If we accept that, we must also accept that until this point in our history the Supreme Court of Canada has been a political instrument of the Government of Canada, the national Government, undermining the legitimate role of the provinces as laid out in our Constitution.
Until this point in our history, the Supreme Court of Canada has been appointed by the national Government. In truth, the Supreme Court of Canada belongs to neither level of government. It belongs to the people. It is a national institution, and it should not be nor will it be an instrument of manipulation for either level of government. That is very basic to our understanding of the constitutional principles upon which our country is based. The Supreme Court of Canada is now entrenched in our Constitution. In my opinion, the institution of the Supreme Court of Canada is a big winner.
There is also discussion about shared-cost programs and that the national Government has lost its ability to instigate, participate, and promote new national shared-cost programs. In fact, quite the contrary is true. For the first time there is a constitutional recognition that the Government of Canada has a role to play in initiating programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. We are not talking about programs in areas of national jurisdiction. We are talking about a role for the Government of Canada implementing programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. In other words, in areas where traditionally the Government of Canada has had no right to be. This enhances and legitimizes the role of the Government of Canada to put forward programs that are in the national interest. At the same time, it allows the Government of Canada the flexibility to institute those programs in order that the needs of the provinces and the people are addressed.
Of course, there are national objectives established by the national Government. If any provinces does not meet these objectives, the money for the program can be withheld from that province. That is a tremendous lever in negotiations. We cannot ignore the realities of federal-provincial negotiation and communication that must take place.
What about the yearly conferences on the economy, and on other issues? There are those who say that we are creating a third level of government. In reality we are simply putting into the Constitution a role for the provinces and the Government

October 7, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
of Canada to play in concert with the important issues of the economy and constitutional reform. This is the ongoing reality. There is nothing to fear. All the people who will attend these conferences representing the Government of Canada and the provinces are elected officials. We are all accountable every four or five years. Accountability, which is so much a part of the democratic system, is the greatest guarantee for Canadians. If Canadians do not like the decisions which are being made, they will change their representatives.
A wide range of issues comes to mind when we talk about the Accord. As we in the joint committee on the Constitution identified, there are weaknesses in the Accord. On that there is no debate. Nor is there any serious debate that the other constitutional documents which are the basis of our country had their weaknesses. There is no such thing as a perfect constitutional document, not in 1987, 1982, or 1867.
In 1982 there was a constitutional document involving repatriation and acceptance of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which excluded the Province of Quebec. What could be a more glaring deficiency than excluding a full third of the people of the country? It was not unanimous in 1982. That was a glaring defect, but that document was pushed forward by some of the same people in the House today who say that the Accord must be stopped because it is imperfect. That is the hypocrisy of those who oppose this document, in my view, for what they may see to be short-term political gain. However, that is a short-term view of Canada which should not be a part of this debate.
What is at issue is the future of the country. We are all being called upon to rise above the temptation to score small political points at a great price to Canada. Today we are talking about a document which is not perfect, but we are talking about a document which is very good for Canada. Those who want a detailed commentary on the Accord itself should read the 1987 report of the special joint committee.
For five weeks I had the opportunity to raise questions and to hear witnesses respond to those questions, and in my opinion all the issues are addressed with great satisfaction in the report.
There are imperfections, but we cannot achieve a perfect document. No Government, no peoples, can achieve a perfect document. However, we can achieve a good document, and we have achieved a good document in this Accord.
It would be very dangerous for us to set about the task now of renegotiating or unravelling the Accord. To those who think that the questions which were put to the committee were not discussed by the First Ministers, I say that they have a great deal of naivete. The First Ministers were well advised. All these questions are not new, and in fact all of them were addressed. Some of the very basic questions at which the committee looked were described to us by some of the participants at the First Ministers' Conference as deal
breakers. In other words, they went through the debate and a deal was reached, the first unanimous deal of its kind in 120 years.
It is hard to achieve unanimous agreements. It is not time now to look for the perfect solution. It is time to take what we have, which is a good Accord, to move forward, and to make it perfect over time.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in conclusion the Hon. Member said that it is hard to achieve a unanimous decision, referring to the Meech Lake Accord, and I suppose applauding the fact that the 10 First Ministers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) were able to come to an agreement. His words were that it is hard to achieve a unanimous agreement or position.
However, at the beginning of his speech the Hon. Member talked about Senate reform and addressed some of the concerns of the people of Canada with regard to Senate reform. He said that it was possible to reform the Senate. He summarily dismissed those of us who are concerned about this particular provision which requires unanimity in order to secure Senate reform.
He says that it is hard to achieve unanimous consent. How then can he explain the facility by which Senate reform might be possible? The Hon. Member knows that as a result of the Meech Lake Accord it will be impossible to achieve Senate reform because of the very fact that unanimity is required. At some point in the future there will be those who will want reform of the Senate. The Hon. Member is from Atlantic Canada. He knows that a lot of people from Atlantic Canada would like to see Senate reform.
Does he really believe that the Province of Ontario, for example, or that the Province of Quebec will at some time in the future agree to giving the Province of Prince Edward Island or the Province of Nova Scotia the exact, same power in the Senate; in other words, equal representation? Does he really believe that the Province of Ontario will agree to giving the Province of Nova Scotia the same power or clout in a new reformed Senate?
The Hon. Member quickly dismisses those who have concerns with regard to this provision as being naive. However, I suggest to the Hon. Member that it is naive of him to believe for a moment that at any point in the future there will be unanimous consent to reform the Senate and to ensure that every province has equal representation in the Senate of Canada. It is impossible because of the very fact that unanimity is required to achieve Senate reform. As some commentators have pointed out, the Meech Lake Accord has put the country in a type of constitutional strait-jacket.
With regard to appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada, the Hon. Member criticized the present process. He suggested that for the last 120-odd years the Supreme Court of Canada was an instrument of the national Government. Surely
October 7, 1987

the Hon. Member, who I understand was trained in law, is not suggesting for a moment that over the last 120 years the Supreme Court of Canada has been a puppet of the political party in office. He referred to the Supreme Court of Canada as a national institution. Surely the Hon. Member will agree that if it is in fact a national institution, then the national Government should be ultimately responsible for appointments to that national institution.
He also said that it was important for provincial Governments to appoint members to the Supreme Court of Canada. I ask the following question in conclusion. Why is it so important for the provinces of Canada to have that particular power, if not for the fact that the provinces want to appoint judges to the Supreme Court of Canada, because they believe if they appoint judges, that over a period of time the judges on the Supreme Court of Canada appointed by these particular provinces will in effect be rendered puppets of these provinces?

Mr. Speaker, first of all I invite the Hon. Member to read the "blues" or to listen more closely when he is in the House. If he had been listening closely he would have understood that my comments on the Supreme Court of Canada were simply that I rejected that the Supreme Court of Canada was an instrument of the federal Government over the last 120 years.
What I said was that if we accept the logic that it will be an instrument of the provinces in the future, we must accept the logic that it was an instrument of the federal Government in the past. That is the point, Mr. Speaker. I am glad to hear that the Hon. Member agrees with my logic.
I would also say that when the Member talks about the Supreme Court of Canada as a national institution he reveals what I understand to be his view of Canada, namely that national institutions are controlled by the Government that sits in Ottawa. But that is not what I understand about this nation. I understand that national institutions are institutions in which all of us, the provinces and the Government of Canada, have a part. That is a federal nation we live in and that is the view of this country that I accept. I know that perhaps there are people in his Party who reject that notion, and that is precisely why we as a political Party have replaced national confrontation by national reconciliation.
Finally, when the Member asked questions about the Senate and whether or not reform is possible, he makes my point. Just a few months ago it was possible to reach unanimous agreement on perhaps the most difficult of all issues facing our country, an issue that has faced us for a number of decades, that is, bringing Quebec back into the fold by reaching agreement on the wide-ranging Accord.
The Member asked whether Ontario would agree to Nova Scotia having as much clout in the Senate as Ontario does. With or without Meech Lake that question is equally valid, for as things stand today with Quebec not at the table, Ontario
Constitution Amendment, 1987
has a veto over reform of the Senate. In either case Ontario has great influence over whether or not we have reform. In the absence of Quebec-with Quebec not at the table-meaningful constitutional reform is almost impossible because you have to get a certain number of the nine provinces that are at the table to agree, Mr. Speaker. When Quebec is at the table, some provinces, like my own, have a natural ally. We have an ally with whom we can forge agreements that can result in good constitutional change for Nova Scotia, notwithstanding that the Province of Ontario may be opposed to these changes.
My friend speaks and reveals a vision of this country. It is the paranoid view of the Liberal Party when it comes to doing things in a co-operative and federal way.

Mr. Speaker, early on in his discourse, my hon. colleague referred to the Quebec referendum campaign. He characterized the 40 per cent vote for the referendum proposition in that campaign as being a rejection of Canada, saying moreover that it represented half of the Francophone Quebe-cois rejecting the concept of Canada.
In view of the fact that the adhesion of Quebec to the Constitution is, of course, the prima mobile of the Meech Lake Accord, would my colleague defend or expand on that assertion? Would he rather not agree that the phrasing of the Quebec referendum was such as to catch anyone off guard who had any form of doubt about the nature of the relationship of Quebec within Canada? Does he really cling to the assertion that it was a rejection of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, who made a similar point the other day in the House, raises a question with which I have no difficulty. The logic of what he is proposing is that somehow the people of Quebec after all of this debate did not really know the question being asked.
I do not accept, after such an emotional debate, that the political people of Quebec-they are people who have keen interest in politics-did not fully understand the nature of the question being put to them. That to me, put bluntly, is an insult to the intelligence of the people. Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to take part in an important debate that affects the lives of all Canadians and that, I think, goes to the very heart of our concept of Canada as a country. The responsibility we have here today cannot be taken lightly, and I know that when we vote, we will all be conscious of the fact that we are helping to build our country.
The debate we are continuing today is perhaps above all a collective scrutiny of what we are. When our descendants, our children and our grandchildren study this chapter in the history of their country, of Canada, they will ask whether we, the Members who sat in the House of Commons in 1987, did

Constitution Amendment, 1987
what had to be done, whether our speeches rallied everyone to the cause, and whether we set aside partisan considerations to make this what I would call one of the finest moments in Canadian history.
When I spoke in the House on May 11 during the debate on the Meech Lake Accord, I said that I intended to support the general thrust of the Meech Lake Accord as endorsed by the provincial Premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney). Mr. Speaker, my position remains the same today in this historic debate, and I will vote for the Accord, now referred to as the Meech-Langevin Accord.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I was a Member of the Quebec Legislature for more than eight years, and subsequently spent six years in the private sector. I then decided to return to active politics, this time at the federal level. My main reason for doing so was that I wanted to make a modest contribution towards seeking a satisfactory settlement for Quebec, so that Quebec could finally sign the 1982 Constitutional Agreement.
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the 1980 Referendum, Quebec voters were promised that if they voted no, it would not mean a vote for the status quo. We were told that a no to independence meant yes to a renewed federalism in which Quebec and its French-speaking citizens would be comfortable, confident in the future of their country and the role they would have to play. Mr. Speaker, in the 1980 Referendum very few Quebecers thought the status quo was acceptable, and in fact, it was not.
We should also remember that the Constitution Act, 1982, did not receive the support of the Quebec National Assembly, including the Pequistes on the Government side and the provincial Liberals, who were then the Official Opposition. All these people, duly elected in their respective electoral districts, felt that Quebec had been ignored, and some would say excluded from the 1982 Agreement.
Today, this Parliament has a chance to keep a promise made seven years ago, namely to complete what I would call the first phase of constitutional renewal, and to respond to the expectations of the vast majority of Quebecers as to their future within Confederation. We may not have this chance again in the foreseeable future, and I submit, with respect, that we should take advantage of this opportunity and do so now.
I referred to a seven-year-old promise. In fact, we have to go back 200 years, to the eighteenth century, to understand the issues, the crux of the problem and the essence of the Meech Lake Accord, which is the recognition of Quebec's distinct identity. As was recalled by so many Members who spoke in this debate in the House and at the sittings of the Special Committee, the concepts of linguistic duality and distinct society are older than Canada as we know it today, older than Confederation or Canadian federalism. Some mentioned the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, where, under section 14, Francophones were given the freedom to practise the Catholic religion. My point is that we have here the official recognition of two religious communities, and also that, at the time, religion and language in North America were intertwined.
Others have emphasized the 1763 Treaty of Paris and the judiciary decrees issued by various British governors in the
years following the treaty. People were gradually allowed to practice the Catholic religion, and recognition was extended to language rights before the courts and to the seigniorial system, different from the British system.
From that perspective, Mr. Speaker, yesterday's British generosities-others would say respect for basic rights- gradually made up the foundation of Quebec's distinct character. But let us get back to the present. I suggest that the Meech-Langevin Accord reflects the spirit of the Liberal position concerning our constitutional future. What 1 have in mind here, Mr. Speaker, is the November 1986 resolution acknowledging the distinct character of Quebec, as well as several points which can be found in the Constitutional Accord now under consideration.
I will add this. As a Quebecer, the fervour with which I will defend Canadian unity will be all that much stronger to the extent that the particular role Quebec must play within Canada will be acknowledged and understood. It is obvious to me that a Canada without Quebec, fully aware of its distinct character and recognized as such by the rest of the country, would fly in the face of its own political, cultural, sociological and historic reality.
Let me state my case for my English-speaking colleagues. The Meech-Langevin Accord, with all its potential imperfections and oversights, is still an important step in the right direction because it seeks to achieve the fundamental objective of bringing Quebec into the Constitution and of ensuring its continued presence. As politicians we must deal with the practical and the possible. We must be guided by realism, if at the end of the day we want to be remembered for more than yellowing copies of Hansard. That is a simple fact of political life. I think Sir Wilfrid Laurier's words are appropriate in this regard. He said:
We are divided into provinces, we are divided into races, and out of these confused elements it is not always the ideal policies from the point of view of pure idealism which ought to prevail, but the policy which can appeal on the whole to all sections of the community.
Realistically, as political leaders in this exercise, our efforts must first be concentrated on maintaining the essential and distinct character of the Province of Quebec on the one hand, and on the other on ensuring the continued presence of Quebec within Confederation. I say as a Quebecer that that is the necessary and sufficient condition for any future constitutionmaking.
I understand the concerns some of my colleagues have raised over other very valid issues and I answer them this way: be patient. Recognize that there are priorities which must be addressed first. Quebec, in a political sense, had been left in constitutional isolation in 1981-82. This problem cannot and should not last forever. Are we going to have to wait for the eve of a second referendum to find an acceptable solution? I say to this House and to my colleagues: we have this opportunity now, let's grab it.

"The very first time I visited Quebec's Legislative Assembly at Mr. Lesage's request, I looked at the paintings on the walls while walking through the corridors. If I mention the awakening of Mr. Eric Kierans, an Englishspeaking Montrealer, to my English speaking colleagues, it is to urge them to recognize the historical fact of the Quebec reality, the French fact in Canada which can be found mainly in Quebec but which is also alive in other parts of the country.
Mr. Speaker, I think it might be useful to look at some of the other testimonies which were heard by the Special Committee on the Constitutional Accord.

"In my judgment, the Constitutional Accord of 1987 meets the present priorities. It will produce a fair and reasonable arrangement. I do not think it will have any seriously adverse effects as far as federal Governments of the future are concerned."
Another witness, Professor William Lederman, had this to say in analyzing the concept of a distinct society: "It has been true since 1867 that the courts have known that Quebec society is, in certain important ways, a distinct society. Mr. Speaker, what can we do about the special identity of Quebec? We could try to avoid it, but this would not change the facts. Even those who refuse to recognize the distinct character of Quebec are so well aware of it that their refusal is due to their fear that, by promoting this distinct identity, they will make separation easier. To them, Mr. Speaker, I would say that they have very little confidence in the attachment of Quebec to Canada.
Today's debate is the result of history. History will also judge what has been said about the Accord in this House. It may not

Mr. Speaker, to be a Canadian or to define the essence of being a Canadian is not always easy, and in some cases downright difficult. It is not always an easy to reconcile our differences. That diversity and those differences have sometimes provoked controversy, even within political parties.
