Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) on his speech on the Meech Lake Accord. I would like to ask him a question about the distinct society of Quebec, recognized as such in this Accord. I know he talked about it in his speech, but I would like to know whether he would care to comment, and I know that we Canadians who live in Quebec have no problem with Quebec's special identity as a distinct society, because we believe and we know it is a distinct society and that it wants to remain in Canada, and I think that in 1980, during the referendum, Quebecers responded to this
appeal and confirmed their desire to be both Canadians and Quebecers.
But I wish the Hon. Member would elaborate with a view to assuring our anglophone colleagues or others outside Quebec that the distinct society provision does not mean additional powers for Quebec. In fact people know what Quebec is and what it has been in the past, and you even recalled historic events . . . Would he elaborate on this?

Mr. Speaker, like all other North American democratic societies, Canada is a society in evolution. Naturally, significant changes have occurred in Quebec in the last 50, 25 or 10 years. One of these significant changes relates to the link which once existed between language and religion, now quite devoid of that complicity which was at the root of Quebec's cultural and linguistic development.
Over the past 25 or 30 years, since the quiet revolution, this phenomenon or this acknowledgment which was made or developed-language being the guardian of faith, faith being the guardian of language-is a cultural factor which is vanishing in Quebec. As a result, the state-and this is what Quebec citizens sought in successive elections-has gradually taken over the role of the Church with respect to protecting the language. Faith used to be the guardian of language, but since we now live in a pluralistic society where a number of cultural communities have swelled our ranks, we are asking the state to maintain and promote this distinct character, whereas before we would ask the Church to do that.
What was once private action has now become collective action. Never through this collective action-first taken a number of years ago, and certainly more vigourous since the onset of the quiet revolution-did we seek to question or jeopardize the rights of minorities in Quebec.
And I wish, Mr. Speaker, that all linguistic minorities throughout the country, official language minorities living everywhere from coast to coast, will be treated in every province the way the English-speaking minority is treated in Quebec. That is the wish I express, and I hope that Canada's constitutional evolution will one day lead to the recognition of the linguistic duality, not only in federal institutions but in provincial institutions as well.
When I say that the Church-to-state transfer of responsibilities for promoting the French fact never did affect the basic rights of Quebec's official language minority, the Englishspeaking minority in this case, I would remind Hon. Members that I once belonged to a government which, even before the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was proclaimed, had the Quebec legislature adopt the Quebec Charter of Rights guaranteeing the basic rights of all Quebec residents, whether they belong to the majority or the minority.
So I do not see why, today, by acknowledging the distinct character of Quebec, by allowing Quebec to play a greater role in immigration, by defining more precisely the role of the provinces in the appointment of Supreme Court judges, by

letting the provinces have a say in Senate appointments, I do not see why this Canadian fabric which is getting tighter, 1 believe in its unity, I do not see why this evolution would cast a shadow of doubt on and change the conception Quebecers have always had concerning the rights of their minority.

Mr. Speaker, the constitutional accord arising from the so-called Meech Lake agreement has transfixed perhaps not nearly as much of the country as should be the case. However, it certainly has motivated a considerable number of people to look very closely at their conception of the country and at the future which they hope to see for it. That is the context in which I want to make my contribution to what is an historic debate.
First, I want to discuss some myths about this agreement which have been presented to many of us by constituents who are worried about the direction in which they have been told this Accord is likely to take Canada.
The first myth concerns one of the least controversial areas. It is that the changes with respect to appointments to the Supreme Court will somehow weaken the federal Government and cause an erosion of power at the centre of Canada, especially with reference to our justice system. I believe that this is a very strong myth because there does not seem to be any truth in that assertion.
Indeed, if one considers the changes suggested for the Supreme Court, I believe they are essentially quite sensible and would have the effect, among others, of taking appointments of Supreme Court justices out of the present patronage-dominated system which has been so suspect to many people throughout the country.
I believe it makes very good sense in a federal system to have a combination by which provinces suggest names for Supreme Court judges and the federal Government makes the final appointments. The myth that this somehow gives provinces the right to appoint the Supreme Court is simply not true. It is a combination that is appropriate and sensible in a federal state.
A second myth concerns the question of compensation to provinces which establish programs that are compatible with national programs though not themselves part of those national programs. Again, there is a myth that this will somehow reduce the power of the federal Government to initiate new changes in social legislation and ensure that those changes are brought throughout the country. On the contrary, I suggest that setting forth in our Constitution a very precise and clear mechanism for how Canada can initiate new social or economic programs in areas of provincial jurisdiction, with the consent of seven provinces as has been the case for many years, makes considerable sense. If other provinces decide to implement basically the same programs, it makes equal sense for the federal Government to have a responsibility to provide
Constitution Amendment, 1987
financing, just as it would to other provinces which are part of the federal program.
The third and perhaps most important myth to discuss is that making Quebec a distinct society somehow detracts from the power of the federal Government to shape the future of this country. Again, we have heard a great deal of nonsense in the House about how that notion of a distinct society undercuts or destroys the power of Ottawa to take leadership in this country in areas like industrial policy, trade policy or other economic fields, which are certainly important to my constituents. If one carefully examines the Meech Lake Accord as outlined in our Order Paper, it is absolutely clear on this issue. It states:
Nothing in this section derogates from the powers, rights or privileges of
Parliament or the Government of Canada, or of the legislatures or governments of the provinces-
In short, this will not shift power in any significant way. Instead, it is a very crucial psychological recognition of something which anyone who has worked in Quebec or has worked with Quebecers and knows something of that province simply must accept as a reality. Quebec is a distinct society.
I tell Canadians who are concerned about this, including people in my constituency, that I very much wish they could visit Quebec to see its various sections so they could come away with a sense of the great distinctiveness of such things as the civil code in that province, the majority dominance of the French language, and the different economic structure of that province. We should not be concerned about the myth of the distinct society being a danger to us.
Fourth, 1 want to talk about the unanimity clause because it is also an area about which a great deal of mythology has been suggested. The myth is that somehow every future decision associated with our Constitution will require unanimous support of the provinces. This is simply not true. The vast areas which make up our Constitution will not require any changes that are different from the present constitutional arrangement for changes. It is only federal institutions will require this unanimous consent in the future. That has to be stressed to people, too. I do not like that. I think that it is a mistake. I think that it is a step backward with respect to federal institutions. I do not think that it is something that needed to be done. However, I do not think that it is a major and significant change about which people across the country should be concerned.
After talking about these myths I want now to talk about what I do see as serious problems within this Accord. There are three of which we as a Parliament have to be very aware. First, the role given to the Territories of the country is virtually nil within this Accord. That is a serious mistake for the future of the country. There have just been elections in the Northwest Territories. At present, there is a New Democratic Party Government in the Yukon which is doing interesting and

exciting things. It is important to the future of these Territories that they, too, should be able to join the constitutional family without having to run this gauntlet, in a sense, which they have to run of all the other provinces before the approval process can be completed.
1 think that this is something which the Hon. Member for the Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) has made very clear to the House. It is something which Conservatives, such as the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), have spoken out on very clearly. I think that it would be a serious mistake for the House of Commons not to listen to those voices from the Territories and make changes as suggested in the amendments proposed by my Party which would bring the Territories into a fuller potential future in Canada.
Second, there are some very serious problems with respect to aboriginal rights. We, as a country, forget far too often the traditions, the people, the tremendous sacrifices which the aboriginal people of Canada made in helping to build this land. I can tell Members of the House that in my constituency great battles were fought in which the aboriginal people, under the leadership of the Iroquois, helped us to make sure that this country stayed independent in the War of 1812. Had it not been for the powerful alliance which existed at that point, this country could well have been conquered by the United States. We could be in a position today in which our independence has already been surrendered, rather than facing at least the last fight in the free trade talks over whether or not that independence will have to go.
These aboriginal Canadians have said to us very clearly that this agreement is not satisfactory. 1 quote from the words of the Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, George Erasmus, who has said to us that the circle of Canada "will only be complete when the rights of aboriginal peoples in Canada are unequivocally expressed and protected in the Constitution, and when that relationship between the First Nations and the rest of Canada is respected". He went on to tell the special committee that the amendment which was made to the constitutional Accord "fails to give explicit constitutional recognition to the existence of First Nations as distinct societies that also form a fundamental characteristic of Canada. If anyone is more distinct, surely it is the peoples of the First Nations".
He went on from that point to state very clearly that there should be changes to this Accord which would recognize this fact and which would, as he put it, establish a renewed constitutional process specifically dealing with treaty and aboriginal rights. Our agenda, as he put it, is unfinished; the process should continue until the agenda is complete. I want to suggest that that agenda of the aboriginal peoples cannot simply be forgotten by the House of Commons. It is just not right for us to forget what we owe to the aboriginal people of Canada.
I would like now to talk about the third serious problem which I see. It is that the women of Canada fought a very
serious and important fight to have Section 28 of the Charter established, which section gave to Canadian women equality with Canadian men. It was a hard fight. It took a great deal of pressure. It took a great deal of mobilization. It is not a fight which should be reversed by this constitutional Accord.
Yet women's groups across the country have said to us that that threat exists in this Accord. We have heard this from the President of NAC. We have heard this from the President of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. The New Democratic Party has also moved an amendment in this area.
It is an amendment which reflects the statements of our members of the special committee who said the following. They said that Senator Lowell Murray defended inclusion of the non-derogation clause guaranteeing that neither Canada's multicultural heritage nor aboriginal rights would be affected by the linguistic duality-distinct society interpretive clause on the grounds of an abundance of caution. They said, "We want that same caution applied to Section 28 of the Charter, sexual equality". I believe very strongly that this House should accept that amendment as a constructive addition to this constitutional Accord.
My final point is simply to say that the Government has so far adopted a position, which I must describe as pigheaded, that it will not shift this Accord in any respect. With a document as serious as this is and as crucial to the future of our country, we should not be prepared to do that. Therefore, I urge the Government, and plead with it, to look at the amendments which we have put forward, which do not detract at all from the Accord, and to accept them. In that manner, we will have for our children and for our country in the future a better constitutional arrangement with which to move forward.

It also gives it the possibility of undertaking equivalent activity with other parts of the country which do not want to be part of a federal-provincial agreement in itself. That is a major point.
Perhaps I could just make one last point. I want to make absolutely clear that, despite the strong hope or sense of optimism which I have in respect of our amendments, I think nobody should be unaware of the fact that when one weighs the reservations against the myths which are untrue, one still has a document for which one has to vote because of its steps forward, despite the fact that it also includes some unfortunate backward steps.

Mr. Speaker, when most Members of Parliament rise they always indicate what an honour it is to participate in a debate. I am sure this one has special meaning for all those who have had an opportunity to speak. This is a very important constitutional document, one of the most important in Canadian history. I think it is a privilege for all Members of Parliament to have an opportunity to give their comments on this very important process.
Let me say something about constitutional development within Canada. I think the Meech Lake Accord and everything which has preceded it must be looked at as an evolutionary process. 1 remember reading a foreign publication at one time in which they were trying to fix a date for Canadian independence. To try to do that is like imposing another society's concept of constitutional development or nationbuilding, because it would probably be very difficult to pin down to one particular date the time when Canada became an independent country.
There has been a series of very important constitutional dates throughout Canadian history since 1867, and I would
suggest that the passage of the Meech Lake Accord will add another important date to the process.
As well, I think Canadians should understand that not all parts of the Canadian Constitution are written. Indeed, many important parts of the Constitution are unwritten, and they, too, make up what is collectively known as the Constitution of Canada.
The Charter of 1982 is a constitutional document; it is not the Constitution. The British North America Act is a constitutional document. However, for those who have studied this area, such an ancient document as the Constitution of 1689 is a Canadian constitutional document as well.
I am very pleased to direct my comments to the 1987 constitutional Accord, and later I should like to make comments in respect of some of the proposed amendments. The 1987 constitutional Accord is about bringing Quebec back into the constitutional family. I speak not as a Quebecer but as an English Canadian from Niagara Falls, Ontario, who is very proud to have been born in that area. As a Canadian I feel it incumbent upon me to involve myself in this discussion and to give my comments on what I perceive to be the future of the country.
As I grew up, as a child in Niagara Falls during the 1960s and as a young adult during the 1970s, one of the most troubling things for Canadians was the problem-and I believe it started at the beginning of the 1960s-referred to as separatism. At least, some of us who lived in the part of the country from which I came viewed it as a problem.
What was most troubling about it was not that there were people questioning the existence of the Canadian Confederation, which in itself was troubling, but that there was an indication that this movement was growing and seemed to have widespread support according to media reports. What bothered me most about it was that some sociological studies showed that many young people had embraced the idea of separatism. We had been given indications-and certainly 1 remember discussing it at university-that it would be only a matter of time, with so many young people growing up and calling into question the Canadian Confederation, that a separate state in the Province of Quebec would become a reality. For those of us inside and outside the Province of Quebec it was a very heartbreaking concept to try to grasp. All of us know of the intertwined history between French-speaking Canadians and English-speaking Canadians, going back two centuries. We know of the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have fought and died for the entity known as Canada because they believed in it. That prospect for those of us growing up in Niagara Falls at that time-and I am sure it was the same in other communities across the country-was a very heartbreaking one indeed.
I have been a supporter of the Progressive Conservative Party since I was a child. When Mr. Trudeau was sworn in as Prime Minister of Canada in 1968, it was my sincere hope that he could reconcile the different areas of Canada and that he
October 7, 1987

could put an end to the continual questioning of the Confederation.
It is one of my great disappointments in his administration-and I would suggest that it must be one of his own personal disappointments-that he was not able to do that. I would suggest that on many different issues-and if we had time I would like to recount them, but I do not believe we have time-Mr. Trudeau exacerbated the situation or the tensions which existed between French-speaking Canadians and English-speaking Canadians.
A hopeful sign for all of us was the 1980 referendum. All Canada watched that debate as it progressed. I believe the whole country was tuned in the night that the results of the referendum were delivered. As one English-speaking Canadian at that time, I would have done anything to ensure the survival of Canada, the unity of our country. I was very pleased that after the successful conclusion, in my mind, of that referendum debate in 1980, Prime Minister Trudeau said: "All conditions are off. Everything is on the table to be negotiated. We will usher in a new era of co-operative federalism with the provinces. We will sit down, make a deal and get Quebec into the constitutional family". You know that was not done, Mr. Speaker. I believe, as most Canadians believed, that that very unfortunate indeed.
Another unfortunate aspect of the 1980 referendum debate was how quickly it faded from the minds of most Canadians. When it was finished, I believe there was a collective sigh of relief. Many Canadians consciously or unconsciously said, "Let us move on to other things". I believe that need to recognize some of the strains within the Canadian Confederation was still there.
I was very interested in the special committee on the constitutional Accord, and the comments of one individual, Madame Solange Chaput-Rolland who said, among other things, in referring to the 1980 referendum and time subsequent:
Inside Quebec, seven years ago, we decided that Canada was our country. We have yet to find out whether our loyalty was well placed. Frankly, in 1982 I wondered if the agonies, the pains, the quarrels, the bitterness following the referendum had been necessary. We voted for Canada; Canada through its central Government totally absorbed in its will to patriate the British North America Act of 1867, cared very little about those who had openly stated their will to remain linked to this country. Promises and dreams were shattered; not a single Quebecois will want to go through such emotions again. You Englishspeaking Canadians have asked during years; what does Quebec want. Now you know. It has been described in five proposals not written by constitutionalists, jurists or nationalists; but by men duly elected by "we the people"-
That is a very emotional appeal and a very poignant one which cries out for the necessity of passing this agreement by the House of Commons.
In putting together this agreement, I would like to pay tribute to our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It was his vision, his leadership and his determination more than that of any other individual that made the 1987 constitutional Accord
Constitution Amendment, 1987
possible. Coupled with this war the co-operation of the 10 provincial Premiers who put aside their differences and showed that co-operation is still possible in the federal-provincial context.
It was very important and significant as well that the Leaders of the New Democratic and Liberal Parties on the day after the agreement was struck gave their endorsement to it. It is unfortunate that we are now dealing with a number of amendments. I will indicate why I believe that it is unfortunate. It seems to me that after the initial support of this document by the Leaders of both Opposition Parties it would appear that they, or at least some of the members of their Parties, would like to have it all ways. Some of the Members would like to support the Accord and some do not. Some would like to support the Accord with a number of amendments. I do not think that has been productive.
When I first had a look at the report of the special committee on the Constitution, the first thing that struck me was the opposition addenda to the report. There was a very pious declaration of support by Members from both opposition Parties. Right in the opening sentence, for instance, the Liberal Party said that its members:
-once again confirm their support for the-Accord as a positive step
forward in Canada's constitutional evolution.
The New Democratic Party Members in their first sentence said that they "fully support" the committee's report.
That is great and good news, Mr. Speaker. 1 presume that would include the recommendation from the committee that Parliament adopt the Accord in its present form. It would seem to me that, having given that support, it is inconsistent, as has been done, to tag on a number of amendments, which it has been said time and time again could lead to the unravelling of the agreement itself. I do not believe a lot of amendments will work.
At the hearings we were warned repeatedly that reopening the Accord for renegotiation would be fatal. A number of individuals appeared before the committee and made that point. From Queen's University, Peter Leslie and Richard Simeon; from McGill, Laurent Picard; as well as Gordon Robertson, Peter Meekison, and a long-time member of the Liberal Party, Jack Pickersgill, all of whom made the same point. If members of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party were frank, they would admit that even one amendment could destroy this Accord, that one amendment could bring irresistible pressure for a second and a third amendment, until at some point some Premiers would say that the whole deal is off.
I know that members of the opposition Parties will say, "Don't be so worried." I see that the NDP claims that its amendments could be accepted by First Ministers without in any way putting the Accord in jeopardy. That is good to hear. The Liberals say that their amendments should be acceptable to the First Ministers. "Should" is not the same as "are" or "would be" acceptable. What strikes me about this whole

October 7, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
discussion is the problems we have had in constitutional debates.
I notice in the opening chapter of the report of the special joint committee what a long, difficult and arduous task it has been to arrive at the position we are at, which is to be able to solve the crucial question concerning Canadian unity. Constitutional development has been very difficult and it has been very easy to unravel the agreements of the past. The special committee outlines the problems with the Fulton formula in the early 1960s and in the mid-1960s the Fulton-Favreau formula, the agreement at the Victoria Conference. It took one Premier after all that work to say, "No, I do not like this", or, for whatever reasons, to back out, and so the whole thing became unravelled.
If history teaches us anything, it should teach us how delicate the Accord is that we have before us. It should be respected. Complicating the thing as well, if we did want to accept amendments from the Opposition, is that the Province of Quebec and the Province of Saskatchewan have already ratified the agreement in its present form. We would be in a position where we would have to change the agreement and have it go back before those Legislatures, ask for their approval of the amended version as well as get all the other Premiers on board. It is not worth risking everything that we have achieved at this time to do that.
Our choice is between this accord and no Accord at all. I believe it is between this Accord which Parliament has before it right now or Quebec's continued isolation. I do not believe there are any other choices. Members of the Opposition must know in their hearts that that is the decision we are facing.
Let me say something about some of the specific points raised in the debates over the last few days, and with specific reference to some of the amendments. A subject that has been raised a number of times is the subject of equality rights. I believe we have ample evidence that the linguistic duality, the distinct society provisions, will not override, supersede or take away the sexual equality rights set out in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I would not mention this but I see the the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) is in the House. She said on September 29:
We do not think that our equality rights are jeopardized by Meech Lake.
They are not.
I agree with her. I realize she had other reservations, but I think that point is well taken and I think it was a point agreed to by many of the individuals who appeared before the committee, the New Democratic Party admits the concerns, I believe, in that particular quote that I have just read, that the equality provisions are not ruined, are not overruled by what has taken place in the Meech Lake Accord.
We read in the addendum to the report, for example, that:
The NDP Members of the joint committee do not believe the linguistic duality-distinct society interpretation clause abrogates, supersedes or overrides any other rights guaranteed by the Charter.
Read on.
Yet at the same time they are proposing expressly to restate the same thing. Why? I suggest there is a considerable risk of having all this unravel by opening the Meech Lake Accord.
It started in the Langevin Block with Section 16.
Calm down, Rambo.

The Liberals would like to exempt the entire Charter from interpretation in light of the linguistic duality-distinctive society clause. I suggest that if this proposal is accepted it will, among other things, make the clause meaningless. If we bought the Liberal amendments, the Charter would be interpreted in light of our multicultural heritage, which is very important, and aboriginal rights, as it should be, but not in light of our linguistic duality and Quebec's distinct identity. It would have the effect of ranking Quebec behind multiculturalism.
I suggest as well that by continuously saying that somehow equality rights are going to be taken away, they are raising groundless fears in the hearts and minds of the many people who are worried about this sort of thing. They have to live with those fears. Yves Fortier, a very respected legal mind, appeared before the committee and said on this very subject:
I believe that those fears are totally groundless. And if it were not for the seriousness of those organizations that expressed those views, I would simply say we were dealing with a smokescreen.
1 suggest to the opposition Parties that they have lost sight of the distinction between the Quebec round, which is what we are dealing with here, and the next round. No one is saying that Senate reform and the other issues are not important. We will get on with them because we believe they are important.
Let me sum up by saying that when the BNA was implemented it was generally conceded at the time that no single individual was more responsible for it than Sir John A. Macdonald. Our present Prime Minister should take a great deal of satisfaction in knowing that on this important constitutional document he, more than any other individual, is responsible. He is responsible for its creation and, I believe, its success. When the history of these times is written, I am sure Canadians, as many do today, will recognize his great contribution. He can take great comfort in knowing that he has done much to unify this country and made it a better place in which to live.

Mr. Speaker, in closing the Hon. Member talked about the great contribution the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made to Canada. Might I remind him of the public opinion polls which show that about 23 per cent of Canadians still have some confidence in the Prime Minister?
October 7, 1987

The rest have totally and absolutely lost confidence in his ability to govern.
You should talk.
Only Ed is on top.

If the heckling across the way will stop, perhaps I can continue. I know Members opposite are awfully sensitive when it comes to public opinion polls and the reputation of the Prime Minister, but this is not the time nor the place to be critical of him.
This is not a place for politics.

This is the time and the place to ask questions of the previous speaker. He should be fuming about free trade because he knows his constituents, the wine growers in Niagara Falls, are absolutely furious about the so-called free trade agreement. Yet this is not the time or the place to talk about free trade and the Hon. Member's political future.

speechtext: What have you got against Canadian wine?
Nothing at all. What does the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Why would you stop drinking it, then, because of free trade?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Can we please get back to the debate at hand?

At one point the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) said it was unfortunate that we were dealing with amendments. He said they were not productive. Those were his words. That reflects his Government's attitude about the future of our country. On a spring night several months ago the Prime Minister decided to act like a blackjack dealer and deal away the future of our country. He started a process which, I submit, was an absolute farce. A committee was put together, and I would like to commend it for the effort it put in, but even at the beginning it was obvious that the Prime Minister was not prepared to accept amendments. The Meech Lake Accord signed by the First Ministers was in effect the final document.
The Hon. Member talked about the fragility of the Accord. If it is so fragile that it cannot withstand an amendment that would guarantee the women of Canada the rights they fought for not so many years ago, then I suggest it is an unmitigated disaster not worthy of the effort we are putting into it. If it is so fragile that it cannot accept an amendment to recognize the rights of the aboriginal people of Canada, then it is not worthy of passage by the House of Commons. Surely he would agree that the women of Canada and the aboriginal people of Canada can be recognized in the Constitution without affecting the basic principles of the Accord, the primary one being the inclusion of Quebec in the Constitution.
Constitution Amendment, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raised the question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I suppose the Prime Minister can take a certain satisfaction and comfort in knowing that he will be Prime Minister for many years to come and the Right Hon. Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) will never be Prime Minister again. I will tell the Hon. Member why.
This debate is as good an example as any. Some members of the Liberal Party say they agree with the Meech Lake Accord. Other Liberals say they agree with it but would like to see all these amendments made. Then we have other members of the Liberal Party who say they do not like the Meech Lake Accord and they are voting against it. That is why his Party is not going to govern the country and why ours is. We have our act together on this issue as on others and his Party, unfortunately for him but fortunately for the people of Canada-
Point of order. The Hon. Member seems to forget that the Liberal Party is first in public opinion.
That will not last very long.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order raised by my colleague from Toronto. It may be true that the Liberal Party ranks first in public opinion, but its leader comes last in the polls.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Can we please get back to the debate?

Mr. Speaker, earlier in my speech I was talking about the long, sad history of the Liberal Party with respect to constitutional change and English-French relations. As an observer of Canadian politics in the past and a participant now, you will know just how much the previous Government under Mr. Trudeau did to exacerbate relations between English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians. He used every opportunity to pit English against French. The arrogance with which he conducted the negotiations after the referendum debate in 1980 is ample evidence.
I suppose it is entirely consistent with Canadian history that the political Party which did more than any other to create Canada in 1867 would be the Party to bring in now the very significant constitutional changes which will, I believe, ensure Canadian unity for generations to come. That will be to the credit of the Prime Minister, the Progressive Conservative Party, the present Government, and all those individuals who have supported it.
I suggest that the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) should get back to worrying about the

October 7, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
principles for which his Party stands and quit worrying about public opinion polls because they will not get him anywhere.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague. He mentioned that if even one Premier were to start questioning the Meech Lake Accord it would scuttle the whole thing, it would be game over. We are in fact to have a new Premier around the table very soon. There may be a New Democratic Premier, but there certainly will be a new Premier who will raise questions about why aboriginal rights and women's rights are not in the Accord. The Government will have to deal with questions on how to improve the Accord. It is not enough to say that we cannot touch this because it is too fragile. If it is meant to last for one hundred years or more, it must be strong.
The Member is afraid of the pressure of one modest amendment. Surely he can distinguish between frivolous amendments and worth-while amendments, amendments that deal with women's rights, aboriginal rights, and the North. Surely those selected amendments would improve the Accord. Surely the Government is not just a collection of 211 marshmallows that have to bend to every pressure brought to bear. The Government should use some judgment and improve the Accord rather than saying that it can do nothing because the Accord will fall apart, or that it can do nothing because then someone else will force it to do too much.

Mr. Speaker, the Member says that we will soon have a new Premier. We have just had
an election in Ontario and it will be five years before the people of Ontario get a chance to change Premiers. He need not worry about that for a long time.
In New Brunswick.

With regard to the fragility of this agreement, I refer to the historical analysis of constitutional development. On two or three occasions in our lifetime the federal Government and the Premiers thought they had come to a deal on an amending formula for the Constitution, an agreement to patriate the Constitution. Those agreements did in fact become unraveled because one Premier decided he did not like all the provisions.
By their very nature these things are fragile. They are very important. The subjects addressed in the amendments are important as well. However, I think members of the Opposition have missed the fact that while to conclude anything in this agreement will take unanimous consent, many issues will be decided on the seven provinces-fifty per cent of the population basis. In the next round of constitutional discussions they will be discussed as they should be because they are important.
